dok_rationale: Part (c) compares two designs against a causal claim, links random assignment, control, and blinding to specific threats, explains a concrete alternative cause, and bounds generalization from volunteers.
stem: Suppose a researcher recruits 30 student volunteers to study whether an energy drink changes reaction time.\par\smallskip \textbf{Design 1:} The first 15 students to sign up receive the energy drink; the last 15 receive water. A tester who knows each drink measures reaction time in milliseconds.\par \textbf{Design 2:} A coin flip assigns each volunteer to the energy drink or water. The water is flavored to match, both drinks are served in identical opaque cups, and neither the volunteer nor the tester knows which drink was assigned.
first_take: Which design would make the comparison between drinks fairer? Give one reason.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the experimental units and the response variable, with units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare how treatments are assigned in the two designs. Explain how one other feature of Design 2 helps the comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which design gives stronger evidence about whether the drink causes a change? Explain one other reason the groups in Design 1 might react differently. State why the result would not automatically describe all teenagers.

answers.a: The 30 volunteers are the experimental units. The response is reaction time in milliseconds.
answers.b: Design 1 uses signup order; Design 2 uses random assignment by coin flip. Accept either additional feature with its job: matched water supplies a comparison while making the drinks hard to distinguish, or concealed assignments reduce expectation and tester effects.
answers.c: Design 2 gives stronger causal evidence because random assignment tends to balance other factors. In Design 1, earlier volunteers might differ in sleep, motivation, or baseline reaction time, which could also explain the observed difference. Neither group of volunteers automatically represents all teenagers; treatment assignment is not random selection of participants.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Design 2 and links random assignment to balancing other factors
Links a plausible early/late volunteer difference to reaction time
Explains why volunteers cannot automatically represent all teenagers

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Calling Design 1 randomized because students arrived in an unpredictable order
Treating equal group sizes as a substitute for random assignment
Saying identical cups alone blind participants without the matched drink and concealed assignment
Confusing random assignment among volunteers with random selection of teenagers
